## Greetings to the Reader. <note>original: "Lectoris. S." where S. stands for "Salutem," a standard Latin greeting wishing health.</note>

<image-desc>A large decorative drop-cap 'M' with ornate floral and foliate scrolling patterns in the background.</image-desc>

Experience itself—that indispensable teacher in matters involving action or creation—teaches us that there is a vast difference between the skilled masters of any profession and the unskilled. For this reason, when we are about to build, we do not run to tailors or shoemakers; rather, we turn to stonemasons, carpenters, architects, and others knowledgeable in the crafts pertaining to that task. And conversely, when we intend to buy or commission clothes or shoes, we do not go to the builders, but to the former. 

And although it might seem to those who do not pay close attention that this principle applies only to the <term>mechanical arts</term> <note>manual trades or crafts involving physical labor</note>, we believe—following the advice of learned men and having observed it quite clearly ourselves despite our modest intellect—that the same holds true in all other fields where the primary goal is either an action or the completion of a specific work. Of this very kind are the <term>civil arts</term> <note>the science of politics and governance</note> and the <term>military arts</term>, which were called by these names by the ancients for that very reason—

—ably. For indeed, both these and other similar matters can be understood through specific rules and taught and learned by a fixed method. This is proven not only by the books written on these subjects, but also by the many most illustrious examples provided by many great men—both the ancients, as far as our knowledge and reports go, and more recent figures. Since these examples are already quite well known to the learned class, for whom these works are published, we judge it unnecessary to present them here at this time.

Furthermore, it is a significant part of the **political** and **military arts**, and others of that kind, to be able to hide those plans which could harm us if they became known to the enemy, and to communicate them to friends in such a way that they cannot be discovered by any means—neither by a dishonest courier nor by the enemies themselves, should the messages entrusted to them happen to be intercepted.

For this reason, both ancient and certain modern wise men have applied their skill to devise several **stratagems** <note>original: "stratagemata," referring to clever tricks or schemes used to outwit an opponent, particularly in a military context</note> for this purpose, as well as for other ways to secretly convey the hidden thoughts of the mind.

# TO THE READERS

## PREFACE.

WHILE I was searching for certain ancient handwritten records <note>original: "manuscripta monumenta"</note> of every kind—seeking to draw out some secret or hidden knowledge (a pursuit toward which my nature has always inclined me)—it happened more than once that I stumbled upon obscure marks and characters <term>characteres: encoded symbols, cyphers, or shorthand</term>. Authors often use these to intentionally hide their work from readers. Because of this, I was frequently forced to set aside the very topics that most sparked my interest. 

Yet, such is the human condition: the more difficult it is to achieve what we greatly desire, the more passionately we pursue it. For this reason, I resolved not to give up on my undertaking until I had deciphered all the various marks I had encountered. Fortune favored my wish. As I investigated the meaning of these characters more precisely and put in no small amount of effort, the work proceeded so successfully that soon this inquiry—

He explains that his curiosity drove him to master these obscure symbols, leading to the successful investigation presented in this work.</summary>

# PREFACE

*...devoted to this task, I interpreted many notes of this kind. When, after searching more diligently for some time, I progressed so far that—having collected as many of these characters <term>characteribus: encoded symbols or shorthand marks</term> as possible—I decided to write a book about them, since the method of interpreting them was multifaceted and proven by the comparison of many writers.*

*But how that was to be done, I myself did not at first correctly or sufficiently understand. Therefore, in the beginning, I faced no small amount of labor to collect several things suitable for this purpose which would give shape to the book. Finally, I committed to my pen <note>original: "calamo... commisi"</note> certain rules <term>præceptiones: principles or instructions</term> that immediately occurred to my memory, so that I would not have to work too hard in searching for them whenever the need arose. For I did not hope that the work could grow to such a great extent due to the sheer variety of the subject matter.*

*Indeed, as I devoted myself more intensely to this matter (for what does labor not achieve?), I progressed so much that I was soon interpreting letters brought from everywhere, written in these kinds of notes, for friends who requested my help. Because of this, I excited such wonder in their minds that there were even those unlearned in literature who believed this ability came to me from no other source than the magic art <term>arte magica: occult or supernatural methods</term> and the inspiration of some deity <note>original: "numinis afflatu"</note>. However, the logic of the context, drawn from the sources of orthography <term>orthographiæ: the study of spelling or correct writing systems</term>, indicated the truth clearly enough.*

*But so that they may see by what rules I proceeded in these matters—rules which I had collected through these days while my mind...*

# OF THE AUTHOR

...having been freed from heavier cares, he applies himself to these lighter studies, and I had decided to take care that they should be printed. But reflecting on how those who release books into the public are exposed to the various judgments of men and the disparagement of "Zoiluses" <term>zoilorum: harsh, hypercritical detractors named after Zoilus, a grammarian known for his critiques of Homer</term>, who are accustomed to testing the sharpness of their own wit on the labors of others: I decided (most kind readers) to reserve this work with me for so long until it might be published as a completed whole along with the class of other books whose names we have listed in the index of our <term>Encyclopediæ: here referring to a "circle of learning" or a comprehensive system of knowledge</term>. 

But at last, for several reasons, it was necessary to change my plan. For since the fame of this work was being spread while it was still "under the anvil" <note>original: "sub incude" — a Latin idiom meaning a work is still in progress or being refined</note>, I considered it advantageous not to delay further, but to diligently hasten the edition. This was due partly to the persistent requests of many friends, in whom a great desire for reading the work had long ago set in, and partly by the stirrings of the envious, who begrudged us this honor because this subject had been attempted by no one until now. 

We, indeed, shall divide this whole business into two parts: namely, signifying secretly, and perceiving what has been signified. We have dedicated the first and second books to the former, and the third and fourth books to the latter. In the entire first book, we have written about the <term>signa: signs or characters</term> by which we signify—vocal <term>vocalia: representing vowel sounds</term>, semi-vocal <term>semivocalia: consonants that have a continuous sound, like 'L' or 'M'</term>, and mute—how they are formed according to the instructions of the ancients and moderns, and both those that are visible and those that escape the sight. But those written with letters...

<header>ON THE KNOWLEDGE OF HIDDEN LETTERS</header>

...they used to mark letters, as is now sufficiently clear in monuments and books of history. Thus, **C R** signified "Roman citizen" <note>Original: "ciuem romanum"</note>, **O P** "it is necessary" <note>Original: "oportere"</note>, and **A B V C** "from the founding of the city" <note>Original: "ab vrbe condita"; the standard way Romans dated their history</note>. Likewise, the sequence **PPPPESSSEVVVVVVVVFFFF** stood for: "The first father of the fatherland has departed; with him, safety was taken away; the strong victor came; he conquered the forces of your city by sword, famine, flame, and cold" <note>Original: "primus pater patriæ profectus est, secum salus sublata est, venit victor validus, vicit vires vrbis vestræ, ferro fame flamma frigore"</note>. These can be seen in the small book by Valerius Probus <note>A Roman grammarian (c. 20–105 CE) famous for his work on shorthand and abbreviations</note> on interpreting Roman marks, which Petrus Diaconus <note>Peter the Deacon (c. 1107–1159), a librarian at Monte Cassino who expanded Probus's work</note> later rendered more complete with many additional notes. They also intended **D I L I A** to mean: "from this stone you will find gold" <note>Original: "de isto lapide inuenies aurum"</note>; and by these marks **D T**, "only" <note>Original: "duntaxat"</note> is denoted.

<margin>Certain authors of these marks.</margin>
Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius (c. 239–169 BCE), often called the father of Roman poetry</note> introduced one thousand one hundred marks of this kind. But at Rome, Tullius Tyro <note>Marcus Tullius Tyro (d. 4 BCE), the former slave and secretary of Cicero, credited with inventing the first major Latin shorthand system, the "Tironian Notes"</note>, the freedman of Cicero, devised figures for prepositions in this manner, and after him Persannius Pilargirus and Aquila, the freedman of Maecenas <note>Gaius Maecenas (70–8 BCE), a wealthy patron of the arts and advisor to Augustus</note>, added others. Then Lucius Annaeus Seneca <note>Seneca the Younger (c. 4 BCE – 65 CE), the Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero</note>, having collected, organized, and increased the number from everyone, completed the work, bringing it to five thousand marks.

<margin>Note 3. On the effect in banquets.</margin>
Aelianus Spartianus <note>One of the supposed authors of the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of Roman imperial biographies</note> also relates a charming and witty story to Constantine Augustus regarding the Emperor Geta. This emperor used a specific device when holding banquets; for whenever he wished to imitate the dinners of Lucius Lucullus <note>A Roman general famous for his extreme luxury and decadent banquets</note>, he observed this custom of using shorthand marks to signify which courses should be brought out. For instance, if he wanted Peacocks, Piglets, Fish, and Hams <note>Original: "Pauos, Porcellos, Pisces, & Pernas"</note> to be served at lunch, he would write **PPPP**. If he wanted Forced-meats, Pheasants, and Figs <note>Original: "Farcta, Fasianos, & Ficus"</note>, he wrote **FFF**, and he designated other foods of various kinds by a similar order of letters.

<margin>Unusual letters.</margin>
According to Suetonius <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus (c. 69–122 CE), biographer of the Caesars</note>, Augustus also—though it had previously been the custom to write by using the letters **C S**—used the character **X** for the sake of brevity...

For among the ancients it was the custom that in conducting legal cases they would denote the matter with certain letters; for they established marks of condemnation and absolution, as was correctly observed by Asconius Pedianus <note>A Roman grammarian and commentator on Cicero</note>. In the notes and eulogies of the ancients, it was the custom for the masters of shorthand to write in this manner: **QERETPIRDTQPDTDDPF**. <note>This string of letters represents the phrase: *Quanti ea res erit, tantæ pecuniæ iudicium recuperatorium dabo, testibusque publicè duntaxat decem denunciandi potestatem faciam.*</note> This translates to: "As much as that matter shall be worth, for so much money I will grant a trial of recovery, and I will give the power of summoning no more than ten witnesses in public." Others used the final letter **M** to denote a thousand; a double **KK** for "the sake of false accusation" <note>original: *calumniae causa*</note>; **DM** for "evil intent" <note>original: *dolum malum*</note>; and

<margin>
* On the abolition of these marks, see Jacques Cujas, last chapter of Book 12 of his *Observations*.
</margin>
**IE** for "let there be a judge" <note>original: *iudex esto*</note>. But the Emperor Justinian later decreed that these <term>legal marks</term> <note>original: *iuris notas*; these were a system of shorthand used by Roman jurists known as *Notae Juris*</note> must be abolished from the law books, because many who were clever of mind used them to deceive the ignorant. Therefore, to avoid such inconveniences, he ordered that the laws be written out in full letters, so that these marks might no longer introduce frauds and ambiguities. Nevertheless, those figures **§** and **ff.** still remain today; the former designates paragraphs, and the latter the <term>Digests</term> <note>Also known as the Pandects, a massive compilation of Roman legal opinions</note>. There are also many other marks which find the greatest use in the books of law.

<margin>
x VI. In astrology.
</margin>
The same practice is found in **mathematics**, especially **astrology**, in which remnants of these figures still remain today. For the ancient astrologers introduced them and shaped their <gloss>zodiacal</gloss> figures either because they sought to hide their discipline from the common people as something divine and sacred, or because celestial signs were identified by figures from the Egyptians (from whom they say this science first flowed on account of the clear air), or simply so that they might write briefly. For they prefigure **Aries** and **Taurus** ♈ ♉ by such characters based on their horns; likewise **Gemini** ♊ from their embraces; **Leo**, **Scorpio**, and **Capricorn** they paint from their tails ♌ ♏ ♑; **Virgo** ♍ from her ear of grain; **Libra** ♎ from the scales; and **Sagittarius** ♐ from the arrow. By a similar reasoning, they represent **Saturn** ♄ by a sickle or by his crookedness; **Jupiter** ♃ by a scepter; **Mars** ♂ by a club or an arrow;

<margin>VII. In chemistry.</margin>
The chemical art <note>alchemy</note> also uses these symbols to describe simple substances obscurely, so that they might only be reclaimed through the study of the wise. Thus, chemists mark <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note> with the letter Delta Δ, arsenic with the infinity symbol ∞, and so too for <term>orpiment</term> <note>a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note> and other things of this kind; to list them all in their various ways would be a superfluous labor.

<margin>VIII. In music.</margin>
Nor are musicians without their own small notes; indeed, they have devised various characters to denote time and measure, as can be clearly seen in their books.

<margin>IX. In the military art.</margin>
There were also military marks among the ancients. In the short lists <note>the *brevicula* or muster rolls</note> which contained the names of the soldiers, there were specific marks by which the commanders could see how many soldiers remained and how many had fallen in disasters. Those who survived were marked with a **T** <term>Tau</term> at the beginning of their line; however, those who had died were marked with a **θ** <term>Theta</term>, because it looked as though it had the sign of the spear of Mars through the middle.

Regarding the **Tau**, and the fact that it is a mark of salvation, we read in Ezekiel: "And he wrote a Tau upon the foreheads of the men who groan." <note>original: *Et scripsit thau super frontes virorum gementium*; a reference to Ezekiel 9:4, where the mark protects the faithful</note> In that same manner, the **θ** <term>Theta</term> was a mark of damnation and death.

<margin>Persius, Satire 4, and the commentary by Anton Foquel.</margin>
Persius wrote of this:
> "And you are able to fix the black Theta before a vice." <note>original: *Et potis es nigrum vitio præfigere Theta*; here Theta represents a death sentence or a mark of censure</note>

If the ancients wished to denote childhood, they used the letter Lambda **λ**; so too were there specific marks to designate the distribution of pay. Therefore, it must be concluded that all sciences have adopted their own characters, through which the subject matter of the sciences might be handed down more secretly and briefly.

> And although they are immortal, they all die as one.
<note>This riddle describes the year (the father), the twelve months (the offspring), and the thirty days and nights (the daughters: white for day, dark for night).</note>

### ON THE SECRET NOTATIONS OF LETTERS
### (BOOK ONE)

We will provide an example here, so that if you ever encounter such a thing, you will not be unaware that it was fashioned in this way. We have converted certain words of our native tongue <note>The author likely refers to German or Italian</note>, broken up or doubled, into English <note>original: Latin</note>, which when restored to the original language imply the same thing, even with a changed meaning. Since an example of a translation into English <note>original: Latin</note> cannot be expressed very aptly, it will not be improper to propose a theme in our own language.

->*A sparrow ever solitary on some roof.*<-
->*I shall pass, but to him the accustomed evil in someone, the summit.*<-
<note>The original provides a "broken" version of a line resembling Petrarch: "Passer mai solitario in alcun tetto." The second line is a nonsensical Latin string meant to show how words can be scrambled or substituted while retaining a hidden structure.</note>

<margin>
3rd mode: An elegant German example of this exists regarding the wedding of the Princes of Jülich.
</margin>

We also express the meaning of a thing in another way through letters and pictures <term>rebus: a puzzle where pictures represent words or syllables</term>. But since an English <note>original: Latin</note> example is not available, we provide a common one. If someone says **ALWAYS LIVING** <note>original: "SEMPRE VIVA"</note>, we paint an "always-living" plant—specifically the houseleek, which is commonly called *Always Living*. If, however, the message is **HEART & SUN** <note>original: "COR & SOL"</note>, we paint a heart, and for the "sun," we use musical diamonds or notes with a clef attached to represent the note "Sol" <note>The syllable "Sol" refers to the sun in Latin and the fifth note of the musical scale</note>, and other things of this sort. Since these are commonly known among the public, we shall omit further examples.

<margin>
4th mode: The language which the Germans call "Red-Celtic" <note>original Greek-Latin: erithro-celtica, referring to Rotwelsch, a thieves' cant or secret jargon</note>.
</margin>

At this time, a manner of speaking is used that is very familiar to peddlers, innkeepers, thieves, and those who circumvent simple folk with tricks. They use many words far removed from common usage so they are not understood, using terms they consider more their own. We see many children and servants speak in this way when they try to weave frauds against someone, so as to hardly trigger suspicion of deceit.

<margin>
5th mode: By the help of syllables.
1st mode: Metathesis <note>original Greek: μετάθεσις; the transposition of letters or syllables</note>.
2nd & 3rd modes: Epenthesis <note>original Greek: ἐπένθεσις; adding a sound inside a word</note> and Paragoge <note>original Greek: παραγωγή; adding a sound to the end of a word</note>.
</margin>

There are also those who permute syllables, so that the last is first and vice versa. For example, if they were to say: **THE ENEMY IS PRESENT, BEWARE** <note>original: "HOSTIS ADEST CAVE TIBI"</note>, they would say: **TISHOS ESTAD VECA BITI**. Or they will transpose it in any other way they please. Others do this by adding syllables...

### CHAPTER VII.

-> *What mute signs are, and how we may signify anything through them;* <-
-> *and first, regarding the movement* <-

<margin>
a. 3rd Category:
Mute signs
</margin>
It remains to have a discourse regarding those signs <gloss>a</gloss> which are mute; for we established this as the third part of our undertaking at the beginning. Indeed, I promised to add mute signs to the vocal and semi-vocal ones. <margin>b. Why they are called mute.</margin> We call them mute signs, <gloss>b</gloss> therefore, because they suggest the meanings of things silently and without voice or sound, being received in a certain way by sight or touch. <margin>c. Examples.</margin> Thus, these signs of things can be found <gloss>c</gloss> in nods of the head, in the stillness of the brow <note>original: *frontis silentio*</note>, in the composition of the face, in the motions of the hands and feet, and finally in the representation of the whole body, as well as in the movements and demonstrations of objects. Among those who are mute, a nod is held as speech, and their will is perceived from their expression and the movement of their minds; for even in animals lacking a voice, anger, joy, and other emotions <note>original: *affectus*</note> are expressed by the eyes and certain other bodily signs. Nor should it seem strange to anyone that gestures performed with a certain motion have such power that they represent the very intent of the mind; for even a painting is a silent work and always of a fixed appearance, yet it nonetheless demonstrates the innermost feelings.

### BOOK ONE

...demands of the will. <margin>k 2. Eyebrows</margin> The signs of the eyebrows <gloss>k</gloss> are also varied, for many things are demonstrated now by a raised brow, now by a set one; for they shape the eyes to some extent and command the forehead. When they are contracted, they show sadness; when they are drawn together, cheerfulness; when they are relaxed, they show shame. In these are the marks of nodding and dismissal, when they are relaxed and lifted. Ovid <note>Publius Ovidius Naso, the famous Roman poet.</note>, observing this, says:

> Speak many things with the eyebrow, many things with signs. <note>original: "Multa ſupercilio, multa loquare notis."</note>

In these, Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman naturalist and author of *Natural History*.</note> says, a part of the mind resides; they indicate disdain, and while the refuge of pride is elsewhere, its seat is here: he found nothing higher, nor anything more abrupt in the body, where it might be solitary. Thus, to raise the eyebrow signifies arrogance; to draw it together indicates disdain. We say the eyebrow is "lowered" when we withdraw from pride; finally, the eyebrow itself is always used to mean pride and arrogance. From this, many proverbs about the eyebrow have been drawn, taken from these very signs of Nature. <margin>l 3. The Forehead.</margin> Many things are prefigured by the forehead <gloss>l</gloss>; for we expand or smooth it when we become cheerful, but we contract it when we snarl—that is, when we indicate that something is troublesome to us. Pliny also calls this the index of sadness, cheerfulness, clemency, and serenity. Whence Terence <note>A Roman playwright often quoted for his observations on human behavior.</note> says to a sad person:

> Smooth your brow. <note>original: "Exporrige frontem."</note>

That is, put away your sadness. <margin>m 4. The Cheeks.</margin> The cheeks <gloss>m</gloss> also have a certain service following these; for that blood, which is moved by the disposition of the mind, when it reaches the skin through shame, is poured out into a blush; when it flees in fear, it grows cold with paleness; and when tempered, it creates a certain serene middle state. # BOOK ONE.

...[a gesture] most suitable, in which the four primary fingers are brought together lightly at their tips, and the hand is carried toward us not far from the mouth or the chest; then, it is relaxed, either turned downward or extended slightly forward. With two fingers we distinguish <note>This refers to "distinguere," the rhetorical practice of making clear points or divisions in an argument.</note>, but without the thumb being inserted; the lower fingers, however, look slightly inward, and those which are above are not even tense. For those speaking something sparingly and timidly, there are those brief gestures where the hand is lightly spread—in the manner of those comforting others—and moved at small intervals with the shoulders slightly nodding in agreement. Admiration is immediately shown by a fitting gesture, in which the hand is turned moderately palm-up <term>supinated: having the palm facing upward</term> and, having gathered the fingers one by one starting from the smallest, is then simultaneously unfolded and turned back as the curve of the hand returns. For one wishing to approve, narrate, distinguish, or signify something, joining the finger next to the thumb <note>the index finger</note> and the middle finger to the tip of its thumb—on the right side—with the other fingers relaxed, is suitably adapted. When we admire slightly, and meanwhile tremble with sudden indignation and pray against an evil <note>original: "deprecamur," meaning to entreat or ward off a perceived threat</note>, we bring the fingers to the mouth once their tips have met. When we clench the hand and move it toward the breast, it is a sign of penitence or anger. We point something out with the thumb turned away. When we show the middle finger, we signify the highest contempt; Diogenes, to certain guests who were pressing to see Demosthenes, pointed him out not with his index finger, but with his middle finger extended, hinting that he was a depraved and effeminate man. Thus, he suggests that something obscene is signified by the extension of the middle finger, just as he says those who extend the middle finger are considered insane. Whence Juvenal:

> ,, He would bid [Fortune] a halter <note>original: "Mandaret laqueum," a Roman idiom meaning he would tell Fortune to go hang herself.</note>, and show his middle [finger]—

Tarquinius’s son <note>Sextus Tarquinius</note>, setting his mind on destroying the leaders of the Gabii <note>An ancient city in Latium, near Rome.</note> because he was unable to conquer them through military valor, devised a ruse more powerful than strength in the following manner. He went to the Gabii and, complaining of his father's feigned cruelty, claimed that he had escaped from his father's weapons and swords. He reported that he had found safety nowhere except among his enemies, and he implored them for help against his father. By the cunning of his words, he so persuaded the Gabines that they nourished the sharpest hatred toward his father. And so, with feigned and composed flatteries, he so won the goodwill of the leading men that his power among them became very great. 

Therefore, a few days later, he sent a man to Rome to ask his father what he ought to do. The father, fearing the messenger’s loyalty and wishing his plan to be betrayed to no one, replied in this manner without a voice, using the cunning of an old man. He went into the garden of the house and, walking about, struck off the tallest heads of the poppies with a rod. Then, having made that demonstration, he dismissed the messenger. The messenger, having returned home, [reported] no... <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely continuing to say he reported "no verbal response" to the son, who nevertheless understood the symbolic command to execute the city's leaders.</note>

### Many things can be indicated by silent riddles.

Example.</margin> which is handed down as having been done by Tarquin. <note>Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, the legendary seventh and last king of Rome.</note> We read in the works of Livy <note>Titus Livius, a Roman historian who wrote a monumental history of Rome.</note> that the son of Tarquin interpreted a message sent without a voice from his father; the matter was of this kind. Tarquinius, the son of Tarquin, <note>Sextus Tarquinius, who had infiltrated the nearby city of Gabii.</note> took it into his mind that the leading men of Gabii <note>An ancient city in Latium, near Rome.</note> must be put to death. Since he was unable to conquer them by bravery, he devised a craftiness more powerful than force in this manner. He went to Gabii and, complaining of his father's feigned cruelty—as if he had escaped from his father's weapons and swords—he reported that he had found safety nowhere except among the enemy. He implored them for help against his father. By the cunning of his words, he so persuaded the people of Gabii that they harbored the sharpest hatred toward his father. Thus, with false and composed flatteries, he so won over the goodwill of the leading men that his power among them was very great. After a few days, he sent a man to Rome to ask his father what he should do. The father, fearing the messenger’s loyalty and wanting the plan to be revealed to no one, responded with an old man’s cunning in this way, without a voice. He went into the garden of the house and, walking about, struck off the heads of the tallest poppies <note>original: "papaverum capita"</note> with a stick. Then, having made this demonstration, he dismissed the messenger. The messenger, having returned home, [reported] no si—

### CHAPTER IX.

->*That speech can be expressed silently through Hieroglyphic marks, and through the figures of things and animals.*<-

<margin>a. The first species of the third kind.</margin>
<margin>b. The Emperor Theodoric calls Chaldean signs <note>original: "signa Chaldaica"</note> as if they were letters; see Cassiodorus, *Variae*, Book 8, Letter 51. <note>Cassiodorus (c. 485–585) was a Roman statesman and writer. <margin>c. 1st Example.</margin>
We are also able, quite conveniently, to indicate what we wish in another way without speech: through the figures of things and animals. These individual figures will sometimes signify single words, and sometimes entire meanings. We find that the most ancient Egyptians wrote in this manner; having understood the nature of all animals, they represented the things themselves from the peculiar quality of those animals through their images. Hence, it was necessary to have a thoroughly explored knowledge of the nature of those animals whose condition they seemed to imitate in some way in order to express what was intended. This will be an example: If we should wish to signify someone who is ungrateful toward those who have deserved well of them, we would depict a dove. For the nature of the dove—although it is devoid of bile <note>In ancient and medieval science, the dove was believed to lack a gall bladder (bile), which made it a symbol of gentleness and lack of resentment. Here, the author begins to explain a specific symbolic meaning regarding ingratitude.</note> among the universe of living creatures...

<margin>b The reason and cause for the invention of these marks.</margin>
The reason why they devised such marks was, as has been said, so that the thoughts of learned men would not be betrayed to unworthy people. For in this way, they withdrew the understanding of things from the common minds of men by various coverings and wrappings, so that a bare and open exposition of things would not lie open. Instead, they were treated as if they were fables, so that the more ridiculous they appeared, the more the mysteries themselves would be covered by a cloud of figures. To the highest men, with wisdom as an interpreter, the naked nature of such things would present itself, and they would be made aware of the true secret. On these matters, there exists a book by Horapollo <note>original: "Ori Apollinis," referring to the *Hieroglyphica* of Horapollo, an influential late-antique work on the meaning of Egyptian symbols</note> titled *On the Sacred and Mystic Engravings of the Egyptians*,

<margin>k From which Heinrich Stualenberg collected and published hieroglyphic aphorisms.</margin>

For these express whatever is desired through silent demonstrations of things. ### ON SECRET WRITING MARKS ###

...is regarded, as if it suggests that one should "make haste slowly," <note>original: "tardè properandum," a Latin rendering of the Greek "Speude Bradeos" or "Festina Lente."</note> and that especially when a matter requires timely maturity, the task should not be cut short by excessive haste, nor dragged out into delays by too much hesitation. Instead, it should be accomplished by maintaining a timely middle ground. 

The reasoning behind the symbol’s composition is this: haste is designated by the **dolphin**, for this fish is said to move more swiftly than all other fish—and indeed all other living creatures—as **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher Aristotle wrote extensively on marine biology in his *History of Animals*.</note> and many others testify. By the **anchor**, on the other hand, the delay of the course is signified; thus, the speed of the dolphin is restrained by the stability of the anchor, and in turn, the slowness of the anchor is moderately spurred on by the swiftness of the dolphin. 

By the same logic, another reminder of this principle is a **remora fish** <note>original: "Echeneis," a small fish believed in antiquity to be capable of stopping a ship by attaching to its hull.</note> entwined around a spear; the weapon expresses speed, while the remora indicates slowness. Both indicate that speed should be joined with slowness, for when one is linked with the support of the other, they bring no small benefit to the conduct of affairs. 

<margin>Another variety.</margin> 
Furthermore, it was the custom of the Romans to paint the **Minotaur** on the banners they carried to war. The reason was that, just as **Daedalus** <note>In Greek mythology, the master craftsman who built the Labyrinth.</note> had enclosed the Minotaur in the dark twists of the labyrinth, so everyone should understand that the plans of their leaders must be guarded, and that their disclosure would harm the author. For this reason, the evidence of such a matter was marked with such an emblem.

<margin>A word of caution.</margin> 
However, the interpretations of such things ought not to be handled too obscurely, lest they always require **Apollo** <note>The god of prophecy; the author means the symbols shouldn't be so mysterious that they require divine intervention or an expert to explain them.</note> as an interpreter. Rather, they should occasionally be accessible even to the lowliest common people. 

<margin>A certain custom derived from there.</margin> 
Hence, words are often added to pictures to help interpret them, so that the obscurity of the image does not hinder the viewer's eagerness to understand. To this category belong the things treated by **Giovio** <note>Paolo Giovio (1483–1552), an Italian historian whose *Dialogo dell'imprese* was a foundational text on the symbolism of personal emblems and mottos.</note> in his booklet on insignias.

## CHAPTER X.

-> *That it is possible to signal by fire at night,* <-
-> *and by dust during the day.* <-

<margin>Transition to the second type.</margin> It now remains for us to indicate the method by which we can signal our affairs by fire at night and by dust <note>original: "puluere." While "dust" is the literal translation, in a military signaling context, this often refers to intentional dust clouds or thick smoke that can be seen from a distance.</note> during the day. <margin>The utility of this type.</margin> For this kind of secret communication contains no small utility; indeed, in these times, for signaling something from afar, allies provide information about occurring events. <margin>Division.</margin> This can happen in two ways: either we show something unexpectedly to informed friends by fire, or whenever we please—even if no prior knowledge of the matter to be signaled existed—we display letters suitable for denoting things by the number of torches, so that those watching from afar, noting the numbers, may understand the messages. <margin>The first method and its first example, concerning which Diodorus Siculus [writes] in Book 4.</margin> Regarding the first method, we read that Medea <note>In Greek mythology, Medea was a sorceress who helped the Argonauts.</note> promised the Argonauts that if she killed Pelias, she would signal it from a watchtower by fire at night and by smoke during the day. Therefore, when the matter had succeeded according to her wish, pretending to pay a vow to the moon, she gave the signal by making a fire and lighting lamps in the open air from the rooftop, just as she had promised. Upon receiving such a message, the Argonauts invaded the palace, and having killed the guards, she achieved her purpose <note>original: "voti illam compotem effectam," literally meaning she was made master of her vow/wish.</note>. <margin>Second example.</margin> It is also read that Magas <note>Magas of Cyrene (c. 317–250 BC), a Greek King of Cyrenaica.</note>, once Paraetonium <note>A vital port city in North Africa, modern-day Marsa Matruh.</note> was occupied, arranged with scouts that they should raise a friendly torch toward evening and again at dawn; by that method, the signal was made so that the news traveled as far as where Cyrene <note>original: "Clius," likely a typographical error or variant for Cyrene, the capital of Magas's kingdom.</note> is located. <margin>Third example.</margin> To friends also outside...

<margin>5. Example.</margin>

It was also a custom among the ancients, which still remains today, that for friends staying outside the city, a return or something else might be signaled by smoke. It was by this means that, through the trickery of Hamilcar <note>A Carthaginian general, likely Hamilcar Barca, father of Hannibal.</note>, the people of Agrigentum were drawn quite far from the city while pursuing the enemy and were led into ambushes. Once there, with a forest set on fire, they suffered a great slaughter; for when they saw the smoke, which they thought was rising from their own city walls, they believed they were being recalled by their own people. As they turned back toward the city, they were slaughtered by the Carthaginians following Hamilcar, who had previously feigned retreat.

<margin>The second method, as the author seems to suggest. One of this kind is described by Cardano in *De Subtilitate*, Book 17.</margin> <note>Girolamo Cardano was a 16th-century Italian polymath; his work *De Subtilitate* (On Subtlety) covered a vast range of natural phenomena and inventions.</note>

If some urgent necessity arises, letters can also be demonstrated by the indication of torches, as was handed down by Polybius in manuscript volumes. This kind of use can be very beneficial; this remedy for signaling is used by besieged cities, villas, and fortresses, and even by lovers...

<margin>o 2nd method.</margin>
<sup>o</sup> Truly, the same thing can be achieved by another method, so that one might learn to speak more easily and promptly; if one wishes to do the same in the Greek alphabet. For the Greeks do not use a few letters and doubled characters to express numbers as the Latins do <note>Latin/Roman numerals use only a few letters like I, V, X, L, C, D, M.</note>. Instead, they indicate any numbers by individual signs using the entire alphabet. <note>The Greek system assigned a numerical value to every letter (e.g., Alpha = 1, Beta = 2), making it a natural fit for a secret code based on finger-counting.</note>

<margin>p 3rd method.</margin>
<sup>p</sup> There are also others who fashion speech by the sign of the fingers in a different way. This they do by pointing to those parts of the body, or touching them with fingers, for which the first letters of their names are required to write the words we recognize as necessary to express our matter, continuing until everything we wish has been expressed.

An example would be: if we decide to indicate **A**, we touch the **Ears** <note>original Latin "Aures"</note>; similarly if we indicate **B**, the **Beard** <note>"Barba"</note>; thus the **Head** <note>"Caput"</note> for **C**, and for the rest of this kind, such as the **Teeth** <note>"Dentes" for D</note>, the **Liver** <note>"Epar" (spelled phonetically for Hepar) for E</note>, the **Forehead** <note>"Frons" for F</note>, the **Throat** <note>"Guttur" for G</note>, the **Shoulders** <note>"Humeros" for H</note>, the **Flanks** <note>"Ilia" for I</note>, the **Tongue** <note>"Linguam" for L</note>, the **Hand** <note>"Manum" for M</note>, the **Nose** <note>"Nasum" for N</note>, the **Eyes** <note>"Oculi" for O</note>, the **Palate** <note>"Palatum" for P</note>, the **Five fingers** <note>"Quinque digitos" for Q</note>, the **Kidneys** <note>"Renes" for R</note>, the **Eyebrows** <note>"Supercilia" for S</note>, the **Temples** <note>"Tempora" for T</note>, and so on.

## CHAPTER XII.

### *On secret letters from the writings of the ancients.*

<margin>7. Type of writing: and specifically in this section, that of the ancients.</margin>
Since we have now gradually reached the point where we may mention those signs which hide our plans in writing—which are called <term>characters</term> <note>From the Greek 'charaktēr', meaning a distinctive mark or symbol.</note>—it is appropriate that we divide their obscurity into two categories.

<margin>Division.</margin>
The obscurity of writing, then, will arise either from the complexity of the letters themselves or from a different method of writing. The entanglements of characters will be treated in the second book; <margin>Type of obscurities</margin> now let us speak of the obscurity which is introduced by the method of writing.

<margin>The first type involves marks which cannot be detected without a specific device</margin>
It seems, therefore, that it will not be useless to hand down the method by which one can write so that the writing can be recognized by no one except when we wish. But because some such inventions of the ancients have been recorded for history, let us first follow their use of this matter.

<margin>1. Example</margin>
Aulus Gellius <note>A 2nd-century Roman author known for his miscellany *Attic Nights* (Noctes Atticae).</note> is a witness in his books of the *Attic Nights* <note>original: "noctium Atticarum"</note> that the Spartans <note>original: "Lacedæmonas"</note>, when they wrote to their generals, devised this type of writing on purpose so that intercepted letters would not reveal secret plans to the enemy.

<margin>The opinion of others.</margin>
Others, however, attribute the invention of this thing to Archimedes of Syracuse <note>The famous Greek mathematician and engineer (c. 287–212 BC).</note>. Two smooth, somewhat long rods <note>The author is describing the <term>scytale</term>, an ancient Greek tool for transposition encryption.</note>, polished by a lathe, were made equal so that both had the same length and thickness. One of these was given to the general setting out for war; the other was carefully kept at home by the magistrates.

<margin>a. The second type.</margin>
Having set forth those matters concerning characters <term>characters</term> <note>original: "characteribus," referring to the shapes or symbols of the letters.</note> which cannot be perceived without some clever device, the next step is to speak of those which are visible to the eye in themselves, but are otherwise entangled in technical tricks. But since the ancients discovered several methods in this regard that differ greatly from the deceits and complexities of our own time, we shall first follow the writing methods of the ancestors in this manner; we shall postpone the hidden writing methods of our own time to the second book.

<margin>b. Custom of the ancestors.</margin>
And so, whenever circumstances or the times demanded secrecy, our ancestors used various ambiguities in their writing. The witnesses to this are **Suetonius** and **Gellius** <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus and Aulus Gellius, Roman writers who documented the lives and habits of the Caesars.</note>, who recalled that **Gaius Caesar** <note>Julius Caesar.</note> used this method of writing in letters to **Gaius Oppius**, **Cornelius Balbus**, **Cicero**, and other close associates who looked after his domestic affairs while he was away.

<margin>c. The first method of this through substitution <note>original: "ἀντιστοίχειωσιν" (*antistoichiosis*).</note>.</margin>
The method of writing secretly was this: the value <note>original: "potestas," referring to the identity or phonetic power of the letter.</note> of the letters was changed, and every fourth succeeding letter indicated the first letter. Thus it happened that the writing was very often composed through **substitution** <note>original: "ἀντιστοίχειωσιν" (*antistoichiosis*), a Greek term for the transposition or replacement of letters.</note> without the usual joining of syllables, so that you might think the letters were placed haphazardly. Between those involved, however, there was a clandestine agreement for interpretation. ### CHAPTER XIV.

->*That the ancient modes of writing are vain and useless*<-
->*in our time.*<-

<margin>1. On the scytale <note>original: "de scytale". A scytale was an ancient Spartan tool used for encryption, consisting of a strip of parchment or leather wrapped around a wooden rod of a specific diameter.</note></margin>
The ancients invented these devices to veil their writing, but to speak of them, we shall begin with the scytale. Who, therefore, in our time, when dealing with great and difficult matters that require secrecy, would safely believe that the risk to their life and fortune could be placed in the security of a scytale? Would they not rather judge that such a trick of writing could be easily detected by anyone who is even slightly curious? Furthermore, who would not understand that such a message must be interpreted in exactly the same way it was composed? When it was written, it was wound around a piece of wood; who would not recognize this? If it were wrapped around one’s fingers or a twig of equal thickness, who would not see that as the parts met again, the writing would immediately and very easily be revealed?

<margin>2. On writing tablets or wax tablets <note>original: "de pugillaribus seu tab. ceratis". These were wooden tablets covered in a layer of wax, used for temporary writing with a stylus.</note></margin>
Now let us see how useless writing on wax tablets is. In my judgment, I believe it is more troublesome to write in this manner than it is for anyone of even moderate intelligence to track down the hidden writing. It matters little that this method of writing has been discarded in our age, perhaps so that hidden deception might be less easily betrayed; for even if there were no knowledge of this ancient custom, suspicion would surely detect the thing itself.

<margin>3. On the stratagem of Histiaeus <note>original: "de histiai stratagemate". According to Herodotus, Histiaeus sent a secret message to his son-in-law by shaving a slave's head, tattooing the message on the scalp, and waiting for the hair to grow back before sending the messenger.</note>, of which we will speak again in Book 2, Chapter 20.</margin>

### CHAPTER XV.

->*On the production of secret marks of letters which cannot be seen, and their method and use.*<-

<margin>a. A transition <note>original: "μετάβασις" (metabasis). A rhetorical term for moving from one subject to another.</note> indicating the reasoning of the method.</margin>
<margin>b. Commendation of this method.</margin>
<margin>c. The method or mode.</margin>
<margin>d. Subdivision.</margin>

We have discussed<sup>a</sup> those inventions which the age of the ancients introduced for covering a script in such a way that the very place in which the inscription was made hides the writing. Now, let us see the invisible ways of writing, which our own age has investigated more skillfully in their place. We call it an "invisible" way of writing because, unless a specific method is applied to reveal the script, the characters will entirely escape the sight of anyone looking at them. Thus, it is necessary for the person to whom the writing is destined to have prior knowledge from the sender regarding the method for exposing the marks. 

<sup>b</sup> Furthermore, because this kind of writing possesses a great deal of obscurity, it will be more expedient to use it for matters of the greatest importance—where concealment is of no small interest—rather than any other method. This is especially true if the complexity of the cipher is also hidden beneath the invisibility. Therefore, so that nothing seems omitted which could pertain to the present subject, we will set down several methods for that purpose. These we have transferred here from our own experiments in <term>Natural Magic</term> <note>original: "naturalis Magiæ." In the 16th century, this was the study of the hidden powers of nature, such as chemistry and magnetism, to produce "marvels" through science rather than the supernatural.</note>, for nothing has been included here that has not been proven true by actual results. It seems not inopportune to repeat them in this place; and although some of these methods are known even to "the bleary-eyed and the barbers" <note>original: "lippis & tonsoribus noti." A Latin idiom (from Horace) meaning a fact is so common that even the gossips in a barber shop know it.</note>, we shall not pass them by, as the subject matter requires their inclusion. <sup>c</sup> There are, then, letters made <sup>d</sup> which lie hidden during the day, but at night, in the absence of light or in the darkness, become visible. Truly, if you wish to design characters in such a way that they cannot be seen unless the light of either a star or a candle is placed behind them, it shall be done in this manner: <term>Ceruse</term> <note>original: "Cerussa," or white lead pigment</note> or another color is mixed with liquefied gum. From this mixture, a material is prepared that is the same color as the paper, so that nothing can be distinguished from it. Then, when the recipient of the message holds the paper between their eyes and a light, they will see the faint shapes of the characters. For it happens by the principles of <term>optics</term> that this material, being somewhat dense when held against an external light, blocks the rays from reaching our sight, creating a conspicuous shadow of the outlines for us.

Then, the gaping grooves are filled with a liquid prepared from vinegar and oak galls and allowed to dry. The egg is then kept in vinegar for a day. Soon, after the wax has been removed, it is sent to a confidant; once he has boiled and cleaned the egg, he will find the characters impressed upon the egg white through the porous and hard shell.

...of this kind, [a person] might not easily be found who is capable of inventing new and diverse modes of writing without a teacher? Moreover, these could be so numerous that a single volume would not seem enough to contain them, nor any person's life long enough to examine them all?

<margin>d. The Solution.</margin>
I do not deny that anyone can invent new shapes for these characters <note>Porta uses "characters" to mean the specific symbols or letters used in a cipher.</note> at their own discretion; however, not all will be of such a quality that they do not cause a sense of weariness <note>original: "nauseam," literally nausea or disgust, here referring to the mental fatigue caused by poorly designed or overly complex codes</note> for both the writer and the interpreter. Instead, we have endeavored to provide those methods which—besides offering varied letter shapes for almost every way of writing—will be easy to use. Furthermore, for those who possess the key <note>original: "exemplum," meaning the sample, model, or cipher alphabet used for decoding.</note>, the interpretation will be even easier to grasp. For if that key is entirely removed, it will be so difficult that it will seem the writing cannot be read in any possible way. But since these methods of writing can be varied in almost countless ways, it will be enough for us to have touched upon some of those which seemed most notable; from these examples, anyone will be able to devise new and even better systems. But lest this discourse be drawn out any further, it is time to move on to the instructions themselves.

*a* To proceed, therefore, to the methods of secret writing, reason demands that we begin with the transposition of order, and in this category, with the simplest and easiest to write. For simpler things seem better suited to beginnings, and by such an order we are all more conveniently advanced toward the disciplines: first learning things easy to know, and soon thereafter things somewhat more difficult and less simple. *b* For this reason, among the other modes of such writing circulated by those familiar with this subject, this one first occurs: it is concealed by the artifice where letters, while maintaining a certain order, are transposed within the writing. *c* There can be a two-fold method of this type. One will be that which seems to be entirely free of suspicion; the other, while it may arouse suspicion, will nevertheless protect itself by its own obscurity, unless a too-curious interceptor, having observed the order of the letters, detects how the connection of the letters is transferred. ## CHAPTER II.

->That it is possible to write secretly through the<-
->transposition of letters.<-

<margin>1. The class of *metathesis* <note>Greek: μετάθεσις, meaning transposition or rearrangement.</note>, or rather, various types of arrangement <note>Greek: θέσις (*thesis*).</note> in general.</margin>
Therefore, so that we may approach the methods of writing secretly, reason demands that we begin with the transposition of order, and within this class, with the simplest and easiest to write. For simpler things seem to be more suitable for beginnings, and by such an order we are more conveniently advanced toward all disciplines: first we learn things easy to understand, and soon after, those that are somewhat more difficult and less simple. <margin>1. The method of transposition, or *metathesis*.</margin> Wherefore, among other methods of such writing that are circulated by those familiar with this subject, this one first presents itself: it is concealed by the trick of transposing the letters in the writing while maintaining a certain fixed order. <margin>A subdivision <note>Greek: ὑποδιαίρεσις (*hypodiaeresis*).</note> or further classification of the same.</margin> There can be a two-fold method of this kind: the first will be one that appears to be entirely free of suspicion; the second, although it may invite suspicion, will nevertheless protect itself by its own obscurity, unless an overly curious interceptor, having observed the order of the letters, should discover how the connection of the letters is transferred. The method of the first kind is as follows.

<margin>Method 1.</margin>
Once an example of a sentence has been proposed, so that it may be written more securely, let two lines be taken immediately in which the letters may be placed. The first letter is placed in the upper row, the next in the lower, then the third in the upper again, and the fourth likewise in the lower, in alternating turns, until the spaces are filled with letters. Soon, once these are finished, two other lines are taken and occupied by letters in the same way, until the whole meaning is completed; from this it will happen that the last two lines may sometimes both remain half-filled. This sentence, first noted in our own characters <note>The author refers to the standard Roman alphabet as "our characters," distinguishing it from specialized symbols or codes used in other systems.</note>, is set forth below as an example:

> I HAVE LONG BEEN INFLAMED BY THE MOST ARDENT LOVE FOR YOU, YET HITHERTO I HAVE GIVEN NO SIGN, HAVING TAKEN INTO ACCOUNT YOUR MODESTY AND YOUR PARENTS; WHEREFORE, UNLESS THE LOVER BE HELPED, OVERCOME BY YOUR CRUELTY, I SHALL BE FORCED TO ABANDON LIFE. <note>original: "TVI PRIDEM ARDENTISSIMO AMORE INCENSVS SVM, VERVM SIGNIFICATIONEN ADHVC NVLLAM DEDI, HABITA RATIONE VERECVNDIÆ TVÆ, ET PARENTVM, QVARE NISI AMANTI SVBVENTVM SIT, TVA VICTVS SÆVITIA COGAR VITAM DIMITIERE."</note>

### CHAPTER III.

->*How an interpreter can otherwise be deceived without suspicion through the hidden transposition of letters.*<-

<margin>

Our next task is to proceed to other secret modes of writing which, covered by a certain veil of words, will deceive the interpreter with clever pretense; this is what we shall now pursue as it pertains to this section. # ON HIDDEN CHARACTERS OF LETTERS.

No fixed rules can be provided for this matter, but it will suffice to provide examples from authors, so that if anyone wishes to play in this form, he may imitate them; for anyone can devise for himself a manifold <margin>6th method.</margin> way of joking in this manner at his own discretion. In this way, a friend jokes with a friend in writing:

->Behold, I send you the head of Venus, and the belly of Diana,<-
->The head of the Robber, and the hindparts of the Dog.<-
<note>original Latin: "En tibi mitto caput Veneris, ventremq; diAnæ / Latronis caput, & posteriora canE."</note>

By these verses, a greeting is signified to be sent through the word *Vale* <note>Latin for "Farewell"</note>, the letters of which are required at the beginning, middle, and end of the words *Veneris* [Venus], *diAnæ* [Diana], *Latronis* [Robber], and *canE* [Dog]. <note>The letter 'V' is the "head" of Veneris; 'A' is the "belly" or middle of diAnæ; 'L' is the "head" of Latronis; 'E' is the "hindpart" or end of canE.</note> There is also the labor of some who prefix letters to the beginnings of such verses which complete a sentence. Such are <margin>16th method. <term>Acrostic <note>original Greek: ακροστιχίς (*akrostichis*)</note></term></margin> the songs of the Erythraean Sibyl <note>A legendary prophetess of the ancient world</note>, which are circulated in Greek concerning the coming Christ; their meaning has been expressed in Latin, using the same meter and preserving that same method as far as possible, as follows:

> ,, **I**udicij signum tellus sudore madescet,
> ,, **E** cælo rex adueniet per sæcla futurus,
> ,, **S**cilicet in carne præsens, ut iudicet orbem.
> ,, **V**nde Deum cernent incredulus atq; fidelis,
> ,, **C**elsum cum sanctis, æui iam termino in ipso.
> ,, **S**ic animæ cum carne aderunt, quas iudicet ipse,
> ,, **C**um iacet incultus densis in vepribus orbis.
> ,, **R**eijcient simulachra viri, cunctam quoque gazam,
> ,, **E**xuret terras ignis, pontumque polumque,
> ,, **I**nquirens tetri portas effringet Auerni.
> ,, **S**anctorum sedes, cunctæ lux libera carni

<note>This Latin poem is an acrostic. Reading the first letter of each line downward, it begins to spell out the title of Christ. In this specific version, the first letters spell I-E-S-V-C-S-C-R-E-I-S... which corresponds to the start of "IESVS CHRISTVS..."</note>

<margin>i 2. Context.</margin> i Next, it is necessary that we discuss context <note>original: "contextu"; here referring to how letters are woven or joined together</note>, for it is of no small importance that the arrangement of letters be observed, so that in the same word, those which require a binding may be connected together. The parts of the figures ought to be fitting, with equal dimension and thickness. The extensions in length, which are produced upwards and downwards, consist of the part exceeding the body of the letter; this excess should equal the size of the body itself.

### On the ruses and deceptions by which this method of writing may be fortified, so that the script may be more difficult to interpret.

<margin>
a 2. A somewhat more intricate method.
</margin>
<margin>
b 1. The technique or method of the continuous connection of words. Regarding the unraveling of this, see Book 3, Chapter 9.

We have already discussed how those who are not yet well-practiced in devising these marks usually write in secret; it follows that we should say something about the deceptions with which such a script can be entangled, so that it may be written more securely and the efforts of interpreters may often be frustrated. But because such tricks can be almost more numerous than can be counted, we will touch upon a few of the principal ones, so that by presenting these, we may provide an opportunity for the ingenuity of others to seek out new ones. Among these, therefore, the first device used by great lords <note>original: "magnates," referring to high-ranking nobles or officials</note> and their secretaries <note>original: "notarij"</note> who draft letters is to shroud these simple marks in darkness to prevent them from being investigated; for they distinguish the words by no intervals, but produce the words in a continuous context, so that the ends and beginnings of words are not separated except with great labor—a practice which seems to obscure the writing significantly. Indeed, we call this mode of writing "joined" and "continuous" <note>This refers to the ancient practice of *scriptura continua*, where spaces between words are removed to make it harder for an unauthorized reader to tell where one word ends and the next begins.</note> for this reason: because the writing proceeds in a joined and continuous manner across the width of the paper, as is clear from this example:

d In these methods as well, <term>added letters</term> <note>original: "adiectitiæ literæ," letters thrown into the text that do not form part of the actual message</note> will take their place. e For this purpose, scribes are accustomed to fashioning superfluous characters for themselves beyond the number of the primary elements of the alphabet. These they insert deliberately while writing, either at the beginning of <term>words</term>, at the end, or mixed into the middle of them. By this idle addition, the labor of those trying to interpret the message is rendered useless. For this reason, in our art we call them **IDLE** and **ADDED** marks, because they deceive for no other reason than the superfluity of the <term>characters</term> cast between the text. For this reason they are also <term>called</term> **NULLS**, because they <term>have</term> <term>no</term> <term>power</term> as a letter, and <term>perform</term> the function of a letter in no <term>word</term>. This <term>writing</term> method is made more obscure in several ways. g The first is that by inserting such marks, the true number of <term>letters</term> in a word is disguised. Another is that the sequence of vowels and <term>consonants</term> thus ordered (which we will teach below is extremely <term>necessary</term> for decoding) is taken away. A third reason is added because those marks might be <term>thought</term> to be frequently repeated vowels or <term>frequent</term> <term>consonants</term>. To this is added another trick introduced by the ignorance of the beginning and end of a word, which arises from...

<margin>i 4. Method of removing superfluous letters.</margin>

i In addition to these methods, there is the removal of letters that we can do without. Such letters are **Q, X, Z,** and **Y**, without which anything can still be written conveniently. Similarly, for **Z**, a double **SS** may be written, and for **Y**, our own **I** should be substituted. There are also other letters which we will avoid with deliberate effort...

...avoid, such as **H, B, D, F, G, P,** and **V**, <margin>k Caution.</margin> <sup>k</sup> In order to avoid these, we shall even avoid those words whose notation requires their use; in their place, we shall employ other expressions that carry the same meaning. The reason for this is two-fold: first, because it will not be very troublesome, as these letters tend to occur sparingly in writing; and second, so that we may deprive the interpreter of the patterns of spelling <note>original: "orthographiae modum"</note> that would be observed in their placement—for without these patterns, the writing is much harder to understand. For spelling can easily open a path to the discovery of meaning. <margin>l 5. Method: Brevity of words.</margin> <sup>l</sup> Furthermore, brevity—not only of letters but also of words—is highly recommended for this purpose. If that phrase of Horace <note>A reference to Horace’s *Ars Poetica*: "Brevis esse laboro, obscurus fio."</note>—**I STRIVE TO BE BRIEF, I BECOME OBSCURE**—holds power elsewhere, here it seems to fit perfectly. <margin>m 6. Method: Brevity of sentences. On the unravelling of which, see Book 3, Chapter 14.</margin> <sup>m</sup> Nor should brevity be favored only in words, but in the entire discourse, so that the sense of the writing is concluded not just within a single period, but (if possible) in a simple word. For it will happen that in such a short piece of writing, the <term>interceptor</term> <note>the person attempting to decode the message</note> can in no way test the power of the characters; they will labor in doubt while searching for words that might fit those few characters. Therefore, it will be advantageous to arrange the structure of the characters with deliberate effort in such a way that the meaning of the words is entirely ambiguous, provided that several different words can be applied to the shapes of the characters in the same way. <margin>n 7. Method: Disregard for grammatical rules.</margin> <sup>n</sup> To this end, it will be effective if, besides a contempt for spelling, the text is written so incorrectly that neither the number, nor the order of letters, nor the true letter itself is preserved. This would be the case if **INGNIS** or **INGIS** were written instead of **FIRE** <note>original: "IGNIS"</note>, **FILIPVS** for **PHILIP** <note>original: "PHILIPPVS"</note>, **FVROS** for **FURY** <note>original: "FVROR"</note>, and others of this kind. In this way, the person who wrote the message will be thought to be completely ignorant, not only of spelling, but of common writing altogether. <margin>o The Reason.</margin> <sup>o</sup> Broadly speaking—

...for it is better to be thought an unrefined writer than to suffer the penalty for negligence once the secret plan is discovered. Of this sort are many ancient words, the custom of which was rejected in later times. <margin>p 8. Method.</margin> 
<sup>p</sup> To this pertains the practice of having double, triple, and quadruple forms—or even more, if desired—for the vowels and consonants that occur frequently in writing. Thus, we may use now one form, now another, for the same character in various ways, so that an outside interpreter might be deceived by the different shapes used for the same letter. <note>This is a classic description of a homophonic substitution cipher, which prevents a codebreaker from using simple frequency analysis.</note>

<margin>q 9 Method.</margin> 
<sup>q</sup> The avoidance of monosyllabic <term>diction</term> <note>the use of single-syllable words</note> also contributes to the obscurity of this kind of writing—words such as ***Nos*** <note>We</note>, ***Non*** <note>Not</note>, ***Nam*** <note>For</note>, ***In***, ***Et*** <note>And</note>, ***Ut*** <note>As</note>, ***A***, ***E***, ***I***, ***O***, and other words of this kind. Since these are more distinctive, they can assist the interpreter in no small way in recognizing the power of the letters. 

<margin>r 10. Method or caution.</margin> 
<sup>r</sup> To this end, it will also help if we take care to avoid the repetition of the same word, lest its frequent appearance alert the interpreter of the writing. Therefore, we shall resort to the use of words having the same meaning as often as necessary; for instance, if ***Quoniam*** <note>Since</note> has been said once, let us afterwards admit ***Enim*** <note>For</note>, ***Quia*** <note>Because</note>, ***Nam*** <note>For</note>, ***Namque*** <note>For indeed</note>, and other expressions in place of the first word; and for ***Citro*** <note>On this side</note> let us substitute...

## CHAPTER VII.

->*Concerning circular writing, what sort it may be, and the description of the instrument which we must use in writing.*<-

<margin>a 2. The circular or orbicular method: regarding the explanation of which, see Book 3, Chapter 15.</margin>
<margin>b Why it is called circular.</margin>
Having explained the simple forms of secret characters as much as seemed sufficient, it is now appropriate that I touch upon another method of writing, so that the script may be arranged according to the order of a **Wheel**. Those skilled in this art call this mode of writing "circular" for the reason that it is composed according to the arrangement of a wheel; for indeed, once the characters are arranged upon the wheel, the circular paper is rotated to indicate the letters.

<margin>c Preparation of the small wheel.</margin>
First, therefore, before we pursue the function of this instrument, it seems worthwhile to set forth those things which pertain to its construction.

<margin>d Choice of material.</margin>
Therefore, a diligent craftsman about to construct a wheel of this kind should seek out plates of copper or brass <note>original: "aurichalceas," a golden-colored copper alloy</note>, for both materials are easily malleable <note>original: "ductilis"</note> and more suitable than any other. For if they are made of iron, they will be least able to be worked, being stubborn against the hammer due to their hardness; if of lead or tin, they will soil the hands upon contact, and furthermore, they will not have durability and are easily worn down. If made of paper, they will be most vulnerable to even the slightest injury; moreover, the exact shape—which is especially necessary for these devices—will be easily altered by any change in the weather <note>original: "aeris permutatione," referring to humidity warping the material</note>.

<margin>e Delineation of its form, page 92.</margin>
These things are sufficient regarding the material of the instrument; it remains for us to indicate what its form should be. Therefore, let two plates of this material be prepared, diligently smoothed and leveled, into the center of <margin>* and into the hole of the other.</margin> which the foot of a compass is to be fixed...

The letter X is excluded, both because it is rarely of use to us, and also because—as Quintilian <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, a famous Roman rhetorician who commented on the history of the alphabet</note> says—we could have done without it if we had not sought it out. For if the need for it occasionally arises, we can use the letters C and S in its place, as the use of X only succeeded them by the authority of Augustus <note>The first Roman Emperor, who was known to use simple substitution ciphers</note>. In ancient times, for example, instead of **ALEXANDER**, it was written **ALECSANDER**. We have made this exclusion so that we might divide the circumference more easily, though it matters little or nothing whether there are twenty, twenty-one, or twenty-two divisions.

Next, secret characters <note>invented symbols used to mask the actual letters</note> shall be distributed as desired through the assigned spaces on the lower wheel. Indeed, because the wheel can rotate, it makes no difference whether we place a specific unknown character under this letter or that one.

<margin>The first method <note>original: "Primus modus"</note></margin>
In the first place, therefore, let the writing that contains the message be placed briefly before one's eyes. Then, let the tooth of the Wheel <note>original: "Rotæ"</note> be set under the letter A, or under any letter you choose, provided that this is made known to the recipient. Then, let the required letter be sought along the circumference of the Wheel. Once found, it will indicate the <term>character: the specific cipher symbol or digit substituted for the plaintext letter</term> that should be used, which is placed beneath it; the writer then records that symbol in his notebook. To find the next letter, he should move the Wheel from its position so that it passes through exactly one space, and in the same manner, take the symbol placed beneath it in that new position and record it on the paper. For the third letter, he turns the Wheel a third time from its place to the next area. This order should always be preserved until the entire message is finished.

<margin>Caution <note>original: "Cautio"</note></margin>
But it must be noted that in the revolution of the Wheel, no space should be skipped—such as moving from the first to the third, or suddenly to the fifth—for in this way both the one who writes and the one who is to receive the message will be easily deceived. In order that the recipient may be able to interpret the writing, he sets the index of the Wheel under A (or whichever letter the scribe used to begin the message), and having passed the required spaces from there, he will "hunt out" the letter for each symbol from its respective region to recover the letter.

<margin>2nd method <note>original: "2 modus"</note></margin>
It should not be overlooked that the Wheel can be rotated to the left just as much as to the right, provided the recipient has been informed of the direction. But if the shapes of our letters are arranged on a mobile Wheel and it is moved to the right, it will be the same as if they were on a fixed wheel and the other part were moving backwards.

<margin>3rd method <note>original: "3 modus"</note></margin>
It should be known, however, that whoever uses such an instrument <note>original: "instrumentum"</note> can, according to his own custom, pass through two spaces, or even three if he wishes, turning the wheel now forward, now backward:

happen indeed, that by the turning of the wheel, some space is either passed over or repeated, which inevitably leads to an error; thus, not only the person receiving the message but even the one who wrote it may not fully understand what was intended by the script. Therefore, to prevent this, it will be useful to know how the writer should ensure correctness when there is doubt as to whether the text was written correctly or wrongly. This same principle is practiced among mathematicians <note>original: "Arithmeticos"</note> using the numbers nine and seven in multiplication and division, so that if an error is committed, it is made manifest in that way. <margin>Examination.</margin> The method <term>Ratio: The mathematical procedure or logic used here.</term> will be as follows: all the characters that have been placed in the entire writing shall be counted; then, from that total number (if the wheel contains twenty spaces), twenty shall be subtracted as many times as that number is contained within it. Then, if a smaller number remains, let that number be sought on the wheel. If the pointer <term>index: The indicator or marker on the cipher wheel.</term> of the smaller wheel is turned to that number, we are informed that no mistake has been made. Otherwise, the slip will be easily detected by its position, unless the error was made twice or more, and as much as was previously subtracted from the number is afterwards added back, so that the deficiency of one number is compensated for by the surplus of another. The matter will become clearer by an example: <margin>Example</margin> If the characters counted in the whole writing reach the number seventy-three, once twenty has been subtracted from this number three times (as many times as it is contained), thirteen remains. Let this number be sought on the wheel; if the pointer stands there, it will be shown by this evidence that nothing has been missed. Therefore, care must be taken that the inner wheel

->is not moved from there, where it<-
->stood when the writing<-
->was finished.<-

# ON SECRET CHARACTER WRITING

It would be improper to shroud such an ingenious invention in too dark a veil. The technique shall be as follows: let our alphabet be arranged on a **Wheel** <term>Rota: a circular device used for cryptography, often consisting of concentric discs that rotate to align different alphabets</term> in whatever order one wishes, rather than the order established by common use. This allows the sequence to begin with any letter as the first, end with a letter other than the last in our standard alphabet, and for the rest of the arrangement of letters to be completely inverted or scrambled.

The order will be of this kind: **D F S G B T C M H R L P N R Q O A I E V**. <note>The author provides this randomized string as an example of a non-standard alphabet sequence that serves as the "key" for the cipher.</note> For the specific order of letters used for interpreting such a script—as will be explained in the third book—will provide the method there; if that method is removed, the resulting confusion of meaning must necessarily become impossible to unravel. ON THE SECRET NOTATION OF LETTERS

The design of the Wheel (if one does not wish to use a spherical instrument <note>original: "sphærico instrumento" — referring to the physical, rotating disk device common in Renaissance cryptography.</note>) can be transferred onto a flat table. This table, in addition to the complexities that the Wheel introduced, will provide us with manifold and more complex ways of writing. For indeed, the twenty characters <note>The "characters" here refer to the secret symbols or cipher alphabet used to represent standard letters.</note> which were placed under our letters and circled the rim of the revolving Wheel, will here all be seen drawn downward along the side, <margin>Description.</margin> attached to our own letters. Furthermore, those letters which in the wheel device proceeded in their order under the numbers, are here extended transversely to the left under numbers likewise placed at the top of the table; they are drawn downward, attached to the characters at the side. By this arrangement, a table is created which shows the sequence of our letters—starting now from the first, now from the second, now from the third, and so on for the rest—referenced by the numbers at the top and the side according to the order of the rows, while the proper order of the letters is preserved within their respective spaces.
